name: Deodorant
lead: A deodorant is a product applied to the skin, usually the underarms, to control body odor. It does not stop sweating, unlike an antiperspirant.[1][2] Odor arises mainly when skin bacteria break down sweat, especially apocrine secretions that become active at puberty.[1][3]

Deodorants work by masking odor with fragrance, absorbing moisture, or inhibiting bacteria with ingredients such as alcohol, triclosan or alum crystals.[1][2] In the US they are regulated as cosmetics.[1] In looksmaxxing forums, deodorant and fragrance are discussed as part of scent and hygiene.

paras: Formats include sprays, roll-ons, sticks, gels and crystal products made from potassium or ammonium alum.[1][2] Antimicrobial triclosan has been widely used in personal care products and its applications and safety were reviewed in 1996, while later work measured it in human plasma and milk.[4][5] Natural options based on essential oils or plant extracts have grown since the 2010s.[2]

Wikipedia dates the first modern commercial deodorant, Mum, to 1888 in Philadelphia, and the first commercial antiperspirant, Everdry, to 1903.[1] Roll-on applicators arrived in 1952, and aerosols dominated in the 1960s and early 1970s before the FDA's 1977 ban of an aluminium zirconium ingredient.[1]

A 2015 study mapped underarm bacteria responsible for body odor using culture-independent methods,[6] and a 2019 study examined how skin care products affect skin chemistry and microbiome dynamics.[7]

Possible reactions include irritation from ingredients like propylene glycol and dermatitis from alum crystals.[1] Fragrance-fixing phthalates in personal care products have been linked in studies to urinary metabolite levels in women.[8] Aerosol sprays held close can cause cold burns.[1]
No studies found testing deodorant for attractiveness outcomes. Related research examines ingredient exposure and skin microbiota.[4][5][6][7][8]

timeline.event: Mum, the first modern commercial deodorant, introduced in the US.[1]
Everdry marketed as first commercial antiperspirant.[1]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, deodorant and fragrance come up as part of scent as a trait, with users asking which products to use and whether skipping them matters.[9][10]

claims.claim: Smell matters to how attractive you are perceived.
claims.believers: Forum users say good scent makes people read you as richer, more confident and more sociable.[9]
claims.experts: No study cited here tests scent products for perceived attractiveness.

claims.claim: Skipping soap and deodorant gives an ideal natural scent after showering.
claims.believers: One thread asks why showering without soap or deodorant would not smell best, arguing odor only builds with days of bacteria.[10]
claims.experts: Reference sources describe body odor as arising from bacterial breakdown of sweat, which skin care products can alter.[1][7]

claims.claim: Rubbing lemon on the armpits improves scent.
claims.believers: One user reports a daily lemon slice then shower plus deodorant, while another replies it does nothing.[9]
claims.experts: No published studies were found on lemon applications for underarm odor.

card.summary: Odor control, not sweat control; the basic scent-hygiene tool.
card.note: Does not reduce sweating; that is what antiperspirants do.

quick.overview:
Deodorants control body odor by masking scent or limiting odor-causing bacteria. They do not reduce sweat.

Forum users discuss them as part of scent and hygiene.
quick.mechanism: Underarm bacteria break down sweat to produce odor. Deodorants use fragrance, alcohol, alum or antimicrobials to mask or inhibit this.
quick.risks: Possible skin irritation or dermatitis from some ingredients, and cold burns from aerosols held close. Ingredients such as triclosan and phthalates have been studied for exposure.
